title: AI fabrication suspected of writing dozens of articles in Canadian publications

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure. A synthetic persona was presented to editors as a human contributor, and the deception operated at the point of commissioning and publication rather than inside any single model. The outlets accepted an identity, not just a text, and the identity is what carried the work into print.

The signals that were available were behavioural rather than technical. The columnist declined video calls and declined payment, and the headshot was later found to be overwhelmingly machine-generated. Catching this would have required an editorial check on contributor identity before publication, and a willingness to treat a refusal of payment or a refusal of live contact as a reason to verify rather than a quirk to accommodate.

The reporting also describes harm to a person named in the material, who was falsely described as a drug middleman and who filed a complaint at an Istanbul courthouse. What is not established is who created the persona, whether any outlet knew, and what the complaint will produce. A belief about a legal consultant being behind it is an allegation, and a filed complaint is not a finding.

reports.title: Exclusive—Fake AI columnist dupes Canadian press to target Moroccan dissidents, and a Turkish 'middleman'
Why we took down an article published under the name Daniel Robson
A statement on articles by ‘Daniel Robson’
Byline or bot? AI-generated ‘journalists’ start to appear in Canada
AI fabrication suspected of writing dozens of articles in Canadian publications

summary:
A fake AI-generated columnist named Daniel Robson infiltrated Canadian media for nearly two years, publishing dozens of opinion pieces in outlets including the Ottawa Citizen, Policy Options, The Hub, and Western Standard. The persona pushed pro-Morocco and pro-Israel narratives while targeting Moroccan dissidents, including businessman Hicham Jerando and former intelligence officer Mehdi Hijaouy. Robson refused video calls and honorarium payments, and forensic analysis found his headshot was 97 percent AI-generated. After Türkiye Today raised questions, outlets deleted his work, though Western Standard waited three weeks.

The campaign also harmed a Turkish textile seller named Fuat, who was falsely labeled a drug middleman for trading with Jerando. He faced doxxing, threatening messages, and photoshopped images from the hacker group Atlas Hacks, and he filed a complaint at an Istanbul courthouse. Jerando believes a Moroccan legal consultant is behind the persona. The article does not say what happens next beyond the outlets removing Robson's articles and the ongoing complaint.
